BACAM: Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging for Multi-Turn Interaction

Abstract

Model merging offers a way to integrate the capabilities of specialized experts, but existing agent merging methods typically require all of them to be available at once. We study continual agent merging, which integrates incoming experts sequentially without retaining previously merged experts. Yet merging in parameter space or feature subspaces does not ensure that the merged model acquires an incoming expert’s behavior on interaction trajectories. Moreover, updates toward a new expert can disrupt the merged model’s previously integrated interactive behavior. Therefore, we propose Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging (BACAM), which learns parameter-wise merging gates from candidate-generated trajectories using expert-guided behavioral supervision. Task-level stability–plasticity control and tensor-level conflict-aware update budgets limit interference with existing capabilities while allowing new ones to be acquired. The learned gates are folded into the model weights without additional inference-time parameters. Across four interactive tasks—web shopping, tool use, information retrieval, and embodied interaction—BACAM achieves an average success rate of 62.82%, exceeding the strongest evaluated merging baseline by 21.69 percentage points. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shuaitongli/BACAM.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents can reason and act through multi-turn interactions with tools and environments (Yao et al., 2022b; Liu et al., 2024). Recent work has produced specialized experts for tool use, information search, embodied interaction, and web shopping (Qian et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025; Shridhar et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2022a). However, current LLM-based agents often exhibit limited cross-environment robustness (Zeng et al., 2024). Joint multi-task RL can train an agent across environments, but requires substantial engineering and computation (Chen et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025).

Model merging offers a more efficient approach for models to adapt to diverse environments: it combines specialized models directly in parameter space to support a broader range of tasks, without retraining on a mixture of all tasks (Yang et al., 2026). Existing methods such as Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merging, DARE, and TSV-Merge have demonstrated the feasibility of integrating multiple task-specific capabilities through parameter merging (Ilharco et al., 2022; Yadav et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024; Gargiulo et al., 2025).

Model merging has increasingly been extended to LLM-based agents, where current approaches primarily fall into two categories: parameter-space and subspace-based merging. Parameter-space approaches modify model parameters directly, either separating shared and task-specific regions for selective aggregation (Yuan et al., 2026) or transferring behavior-critical neurons identified from activation patterns (Feng et al., 2026). Subspace-based approaches preserve existing agent behavior by identifying behavior-critical feature subspaces and projecting new task vectors into the corresponding null spaces (Wang et al., 2026). These approaches require jointly available experts for batch merging; repeating the merge as new tasks arise becomes costly (Tang et al., 2025).

To this end, we formulate a novel task: continual agent merging for interactive environments. As shown in Figure 1, batch merging combines all experts at once, whereas continual merging updates the current model as new experts arrive without retaining earlier experts.

This continual setting presents two coupled challenges. First, merging in parameter space or feature subspaces does not ensure that the merged model acquires the incoming expert’s interactive capability. The merged model’s actions determine subsequent observations and may lead to trajectories different from those of the expert. Parameter merging must therefore transfer the expert’s behavior to the trajectories induced by the merged model itself. Second, each merge moves the parameters toward the incoming expert, while previously integrated capabilities are encoded in the current merged model. Even a small parameter change can alter an action on an earlier task and redirect the subsequent trajectory, disrupting established interactive behavior. The merge must therefore acquire the incoming expert’s capability while preserving the current model’s established interactive behavior.

To address these challenges, we propose Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging (BACAM), which learns parameter-wise gates between the current merged model and each incoming expert. BACAM comprises two components. First, task-level stability–plasticity control supervises gate updates on candidate-generated interaction trajectories: the incoming expert guides new-task acquisition, while the current merged model constrains behavioral drift on earlier tasks. Second, tensor-level conflict-aware plasticity budgeting assigns smaller update budgets to tensors where these goals conflict, protecting existing capabilities while allowing adaptation in less sensitive regions. Together, these components enable behavior-aware and conflict-sensitive continual agent merging. We evaluate BACAM across expert counts and merging orders. Under the default order, BACAM has the highest Avg SR at each expert count and exceeds WUDI-Merging by 21.69 percentage points after four experts. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We formulate continual agent merging for multi-turn interactive tasks and assess capability acquisition and retention over complete interaction trajectories.

  2. 2.

    We introduce BACAM, which learns parameter-wise merging gates from behavioral supervision on candidate-generated trajectories. Task-level constraints guide new-task acquisition while limiting drift on earlier tasks, and tensor-level conflict-aware budgets restrict updates where these goals interfere.

  3. 3.

    Across four interactive tasks, BACAM achieves the highest average success rate among the evaluated merging methods at each stage of the default merging sequence. We also track capability acquisition and retention across four arrival orders and use ablations to measure the contribution of each control component.

2 Related Work

Model Merging.

Model merging combines specialized models in parameter space to integrate their capabilities (Yang et al., 2026). Task Arithmetic represents fine-tuning updates as task vectors and adds them together (Ilharco et al., 2022), but direct addition can cause interference. TIES-Merging trims small updates and resolves sign conflicts (Yadav et al., 2023), while DARE sparsifies updates before merging (Yu et al., 2024). TSV-Merge instead reduces interference by decorrelating task singular vectors (Gargiulo et al., 2025). Rather than applying predefined rules to task updates, another line of work optimizes the merge directly: WUDI-Merging minimizes interference among task vectors (Cheng et al., 2025), AdaMerging optimizes coefficients using prediction entropy (Yang et al., 2024b), and Expert Merging learns coefficients through unsupervised expert alignment (Zhang et al., 2026). These methods improve the combination of model parameters, but do not directly assess whether an agent retains its behavior over multi-turn interactions.

Agent Model Merging.

Agent model merging applies these ideas to specialized LLM agents. RAM separates sparse RL task vectors into shared and task-specific regions, then selectively aggregates them to preserve domain-specific behavior (Yuan et al., 2026). ARM identifies role-conditioned neurons from activation patterns and transfers them to a generalist agent (Feng et al., 2026). M2A takes a subspace approach: it identifies behavior-critical features and projects new task vectors into their null spaces to limit disruption of existing capabilities (Wang et al., 2026). These methods merge jointly available source models and do not address sequentially arriving experts.

Continual Model Merging.

Continual model merging integrates task-specific models sequentially. OPCM projects incoming task vectors onto directions orthogonal to accumulated updates (Tang et al., 2025). DOP applies separate projections to protect existing knowledge and acquire new capabilities without task data (Yang et al., 2025). MINGLE combines gated low-rank experts for test-time adaptation (Qiu et al., 2025), while NUFILT couples null-space filtering with a lightweight adapter to recover useful new-task directions (Qiu et al., 2026). These methods primarily evaluate non-interactive prediction tasks. Whether they preserve an agent’s earlier capabilities over full interactions remains unclear: one changed action can redirect the subsequent observations and decisions.

3 Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging

3.1 Problem Definition

We consider an ordered sequence of interactive tasks τ=1,…,T\tau=1,\ldots,T, such as web shopping, tool use, information retrieval, and embodied interaction. Task τ\tau provides a specialized expert EτE_{\tau}, an interaction environment, and unlabeled instances 𝒟τ\mathcal{D}_{\tau} without accompanying ground-truth responses or expert demonstration trajectories. All experts share the same architecture and tokenizer. Let MtM_{t} be the merged model at stage tt. We start with M1=E1M_{1}=E_{1}. At each subsequent stage t≥2t\geq 2, we merge the current model Mt−1M_{t-1} with the incoming expert EtE_{t} to obtain MtM_{t}. Earlier experts are no longer retained, but the instances and environments for all integrated tasks remain available for collecting trajectories, following the idea of replaying retained task inputs (Marouf et al., 2025). Behavioral supervision is provided by the incoming expert and the current merged model on candidate-generated trajectories.

The goal is for MtM_{t} to acquire EtE_{t}’s capability on the new task while preserving Mt−1M_{t-1}’s capabilities on every earlier task τ<t\tau<t. We evaluate both acquisition and preservation in multi-turn interactions. Appendix A gives the formal interaction model.

3.2 Framework Overview

BACAM constructs a merged candidate from Mt−1M_{t-1} and EtE_{t} and rolls it out on the new and earlier tasks (Figure 2). Within task-level control, New-task Plasticity Control (NPC) uses EtE_{t} to guide capability acquisition, while Old-task Stability Control (OSC) uses Mt−1M_{t-1} to limit behavioral drift on earlier tasks. Tensor-Level Conflict-Aware Plasticity Budgeting (CAPB) restricts gate updates in tensors where these two goals conflict.

To define the merged candidate, let θt−1merged\theta_{t-1}^{\mathrm{merged}} and θt\theta_{t} denote the parameters of Mt−1M_{t-1} and EtE_{t}, respectively, and set Δ​θt=θt−θt−1merged\Delta\theta_{t}=\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}^{\mathrm{merged}}. A parameter-wise gate gg determines the candidate’s weights:

θtmerged​(g)=θt−1merged+g⊙Δ​θt,g∈[0,1]|θ|.\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g)=\theta_{t-1}^{\mathrm{merged}}+g\odot\Delta\theta_{t},\qquad g\in[0,1]^{|\theta|}. (1)

The current merged model and incoming expert remain frozen, and only gg is optimized. For parameter jj, gj=0g_{j}=0 retains the old-model value and gj=1g_{j}=1 selects the new-expert value. Compared with coarse-grained merging coefficients, the parameter-wise gate can express different stability–plasticity trade-offs within the same tensor (Yang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2026).

3.3 Task-Level Stability–Plasticity Control

Behavioral supervision on candidate trajectories.

The candidate’s actions affect subsequent observations, so fixed prompts or expert-generated trajectories may not cover the histories it visits. For each task τ≤t\tau\leq t, we roll out the candidate policy πθtmerged​(g)\pi_{\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g)} in the task environment using instances from 𝒟τ\mathcal{D}_{\tau}, obtaining trajectories ℛτ\mathcal{R}_{\tau}. We write the decision points of each trajectory ξ\xi as ((xi,yi))i=1|ξ|((x_{i},y_{i}))_{i=1}^{|\xi|}, where xix_{i} contains the interaction history and current observation, and yiy_{i} is the candidate’s reasoning and action. The incoming expert supervises task tt; the current merged model supervises tasks τ<t\tau<t. At response token kk of decision point ii, the candidate and teacher distributions are

pg,i,k\displaystyle p_{g,i,k} =πθtmerged​(g)(⋅∣xi,yi,<k),\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g)}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i,<k}), (2)
qt,i,k\displaystyle q_{t,i,k} =πθt(⋅∣xi,yi,<k),\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i,<k}),
qτ,i,k\displaystyle q_{\tau,i,k} =πθt−1merged(⋅∣xi,yi,<k),τ<t.\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta_{t-1}^{\mathrm{merged}}}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i,<k}),\quad\tau<t.

At each token, the candidate and teacher are evaluated on the same candidate-generated prefix; only the candidate interacts with the environment (Agarwal et al., 2024; Song and Zheng, 2026).

Behavior-aware loss aggregation.

To form task-level losses from these distributions, we account for the different roles of response tokens. Reasoning text affects the environment indirectly, whereas search queries, function calls, and environment actions directly determine the next observation. Using task-format markers, we partition the response positions at decision point ii into critical behavior tokens CiC_{i} and remaining tokens NiN_{i}. Let ℬi⊆{Ci,Ni}\mathcal{B}_{i}\subseteq\{C_{i},N_{i}\} contain the nonempty groups. For a token-level divergence DD, we average uniformly within each group and then across the available groups:

ℓiD​(g,qτ)=𝔼B∈ℬi​𝔼k∈B​[D⁡(pg,i,k,qτ,i,k)].\ell_{i}^{D}(g;q_{\tau})=\mathbb{E}_{B\in\mathcal{B}_{i}}\mathbb{E}_{k\in B}\left[D\!\left(p_{g,i,k},q_{\tau,i,k}\right)\right]. (3)

This prevents ordinary text tokens from overwhelming sparse but consequential action tokens. We also give each trajectory equal weight:

ZτD​(g,qτ)=𝔼ξ∈ℛτ​𝔼i=1|ξ|​[ℓiD​(g,qτ)],Z_{\tau}^{D}(g;q_{\tau})=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\in\mathcal{R}_{\tau}}\mathbb{E}_{i=1}^{|\xi|}\left[\ell_{i}^{D}(g;q_{\tau})\right], (4)

Within a trajectory, we average over its decision points, so longer interactions do not dominate the loss. We use this aggregation for both P⁡(g)P(g) and Sτ​(g)S_{\tau}(g), with different KL directions for the new and earlier tasks.

Plasticity and stability losses.

For NPC, we use forward KL from the incoming expert to the candidate:

P(g)=ZtDF(g;qt),DF(pg,i,k,qt,i,k)=DKL(qt,i,k∥pg,i,k),P(g)=Z_{t}^{D_{\mathrm{F}}}(g;q_{t}),\qquad D_{\mathrm{F}}(p_{g,i,k},q_{t,i,k})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{t,i,k}\|p_{g,i,k}), (5)

This penalizes the candidate when it assigns insufficient probability to tokens preferred by the incoming expert, encouraging it to acquire the expert’s behavior on the histories it visits (Agarwal et al., 2024).

For OSC on each earlier task τ<t\tau<t, we use reverse KL from the candidate to the current merged model:

Sτ(g)=ZτDR(g;qτ),DR(pg,i,k,qτ,i,k)=DKL(pg,i,k∥qτ,i,k),S_{\tau}(g)=Z_{\tau}^{D_{\mathrm{R}}}(g;q_{\tau}),\qquad D_{\mathrm{R}}(p_{g,i,k},q_{\tau,i,k})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{g,i,k}\|q_{\tau,i,k}), (6)

This penalizes probability mass assigned to tokens that the current merged model considers unlikely. Limiting Sτ​(g)S_{\tau}(g) therefore constrains behavioral drift on task τ\tau and provides the stability signal for preserving its previously integrated capability (Gu et al., 2024).

Task-level objective and optimization.

To acquire the incoming capability while preserving earlier ones, BACAM minimizes P⁡(g)P(g) subject to a behavioral-drift budget ϵ\epsilon for each old task:

ming∈[0,1]|θ|⁡P⁡(g)s.t.Sτ​(g)≤ϵ,∀τ<t,\min_{g\in[0,1]^{|\theta|}}P(g)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad S_{\tau}(g)\leq\epsilon,\quad\forall\tau<t, (7)

We optimize this constrained objective using a Lagrangian with one nonnegative multiplier λτ\lambda_{\tau} for each old task:

ℒ⁡(g,λ)=P⁡(g)+∑τ<tλτ​(Sτ​(g)−ϵ),\mathcal{L}(g,\lambda)=P(g)+\sum_{\tau<t}\lambda_{\tau}\bigl(S_{\tau}(g)-\epsilon\bigr), (8)

Gate updates descend ℒ\mathcal{L}, while projected dual-ascent steps increase λτ\lambda_{\tau} when Sτ​(g)>ϵS_{\tau}(g)>\epsilon and decrease it when the drift is below budget. Each old task therefore adjusts its own stability weight as merging proceeds. The update rules are summarized in Algorithm 1 and detailed in Appendix A.3.

3.4 Tensor-Level Conflict-Aware Plasticity Budgeting

Each task-level multiplier sets one stability weight for an old task across the whole model. It cannot distinguish tensors in which acquiring the new task would disrupt that task. CAPB therefore assigns a separate plasticity budget to each tensor to limit such updates.

Tensor-level conflict estimation.

We estimate local conflict after a temporary step toward the new task. During each refresh round, the collected trajectories remain fixed while we compute gradients. Let gstartg_{\mathrm{start}} be the current gate and v=∇gP​(gstart)v=\nabla_{g}P(g_{\mathrm{start}}) the new-task gradient. The probe gate is

gprobe=clip⁡(gstart−ηprobe​v‖v‖2,0,1).g_{\mathrm{probe}}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(g_{\mathrm{start}}-\eta_{\mathrm{probe}}\frac{v}{\|v\|_{2}},0,1\right). (9)

Here, clip⁡(⋅,0,1)\operatorname{clip}(\cdot,0,1) clips each gate component to [0,1][0,1]. Let vhv_{h} be the part of vv corresponding to tensor hh. At gprobeg_{\mathrm{probe}}, we compute the old-task stability gradient sτ,h=∇ghSτ​(gprobe)s_{\tau,h}=\nabla_{g_{h}}S_{\tau}(g_{\mathrm{probe}}). A negative inner product ⟨vh,sτ,h⟩\langle v_{h},s_{\tau,h}\rangle means that further movement along −vh-v_{h} would locally increase old-task drift. We measure this conflict by

cτ,h=max⁡(0,−⟨vh,sτ,h⟩‖vh‖2​‖sτ,h‖2+δ).c_{\tau,h}=\max\!\left(0,\frac{-\langle v_{h},s_{\tau,h}\rangle}{\|v_{h}\|_{2}\|s_{\tau,h}\|_{2}+\delta}\right). (10)

Here, δ>0\delta>0 is a small constant for numerical stability.

Plasticity budget construction.

The conflict score captures direction but not how strongly the old task responds to changes in tensor hh. We therefore combine cτ,hc_{\tau,h} with the gradient magnitudes Vh=‖vh‖2V_{h}=\|v_{h}\|_{2} and Uτ,h=‖sτ,h‖2U_{\tau,h}=\|s_{\tau,h}\|_{2}:

bτ,h=1−cτ,h​Uτ,hVh+Uτ,h+δ,bh=minτ<t⁡bτ,h.b_{\tau,h}=1-\frac{c_{\tau,h}U_{\tau,h}}{V_{h}+U_{\tau,h}+\delta},\qquad b_{h}=\min_{\tau<t}b_{\tau,h}. (11)

The budget satisfies 0≤bh≤10\leq b_{h}\leq 1. Tensors with no detected conflict have bh=1b_{h}=1; an opposing gradient and stronger old-task sensitivity reduce the budget. Taking the minimum gives each tensor the most restrictive budget across old tasks. The probe only estimates these budgets; the actual gate updates start from gstartg_{\mathrm{start}}.

Budgeted gate updates.

Let Δ​g\Delta g be the normalized descent step computed from the task-level objective ℒ\mathcal{L}, as in Algorithm 1. We apply the tensor budgets only to positive gate updates, which move parameters toward the new expert:

Δ​gsafe,h=bh​[Δ​gh]++[Δ​gh]−,gh←clip⁡(gh+Δ​gsafe,h,0,1),\Delta g_{\mathrm{safe},h}=b_{h}[\Delta g_{h}]_{+}+[\Delta g_{h}]_{-},\qquad g_{h}\leftarrow\operatorname{clip}\!\left(g_{h}+\Delta g_{\mathrm{safe},h},0,1\right), (12)

where [z]+=max⁡(z,0)[z]_{+}=\max(z,0) and [z]−=min⁡(z,0)[z]_{-}=\min(z,0) are applied elementwise. Negative updates move the gate back toward the old model and are therefore not restricted by the plasticity budget.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the rollout, budget, and gate-update steps. After NN refresh rounds, the learned gate is folded into the model parameters, introducing no additional inference-time parameters or computation.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Backbones.

We merge four specialized experts built on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024a): ReSearch for information retrieval (Chen et al., 2025), ToolRL for tool use (Qian et al., 2025), and two GiGPO experts for WebShop and ALFWorld (Feng et al., 2025). They share the same architecture and tokenizer. The default merging order is WebShop →\rightarrow Tool →\rightarrow Search →\rightarrow ALFWorld, with the WebShop expert as the initial model.

Evaluations.

We evaluate shopping with WebShop (Yao et al., 2022a), tool use with BFCL v3 multi_turn_base (Patil et al., 2025), information retrieval with MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022), and embodied interaction with ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020). The primary metric is success rate (SR, % ↑\uparrow) under each benchmark’s criterion; for ALFWorld, we report both IID (valid_seen) and OOD (valid_unseen) SR. Avg SR is the mean of the five reported columns, counting the two ALFWorld splits separately. We also report WebShop task score (TS ↑\uparrow) and average interaction steps (Round ↓\downarrow) for WebShop and ALFWorld. All methods use the same held-out instances and benchmark settings. Dataset sizes, scoring rules, and generation settings are given in Appendix B.

Baselines.

We compare methods with different access to task instances during merging. Weight averaging (Wortsman et al., 2022), Task Arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2022), TIES-Merging (Yadav et al., 2023), DARE variants (Yu et al., 2024), TSV-Merge (Gargiulo et al., 2025), Iso-C (Marczak et al., 2025), WUDI-Merging (Cheng et al., 2025), RAM and RAM++ (Yuan et al., 2026), OPCM (Tang et al., 2025), and NUFILT (Qiu et al., 2026) operate on model parameters without task instances. AdaMerging and AdaMerging++ (Yang et al., 2024b) instead minimize prediction entropy on unlabeled prompts, while Expert Merging (Zhang et al., 2026) aligns hidden states and output distributions using unlabeled calibration data. We also evaluate the base model and each individual expert. The final-model comparison includes both batch and continual methods using the same four experts. Table 5 details their merge-time data and supervision.

Implementation details.

We select 256 candidate-generated states per task stream in each round and 24 trajectories per stream for local probing. The gate learning rate is 2×10−22\times 10^{-2} with cosine decay, and the stability budget is ϵ=5×10−3\epsilon=5\times 10^{-3}. The dual update uses ηλ=λmax=1\eta_{\lambda}=\lambda_{\max}=1. Training uses 8×8\times RTX 5090 GPUs. Additional settings are provided in Appendix B.

4.2 Performance Comparison

Overall performance.

BACAM achieves an Avg SR of 62.82%, exceeding the strongest measured baseline, WUDI-Merging, by 21.69 percentage points (Table 1). The largest differences are on Tool and WebShop: BACAM reaches 38.00% Tool SR, compared with 0–2% for the evaluated merging baselines, and 77.20% WebShop SR, compared with 39.40% for TSV-Merge. On Search, BACAM scores 23.75%, below WUDI-Merging’s 25.14%.

Comparison with specialists.

BACAM remains close to the WebShop and Search experts, trailing them by 0.80 and 0.59 percentage points, respectively. Tool SR exceeds its expert by 8.00 points, whereas ALFWorld IID/OOD SR remains 10.00/4.47 points below its expert. Additional TS and Round results are reported in Table 8.

Two- and three-expert merging.

Appendix Table 6 reports the first two merging stages in the default order. After adding Tool, BACAM reaches 32.00% Tool SR while retaining 78.60% WebShop SR; after adding Search, these scores are 37.00% and 78.40%, with 24.10% Search SR. The other merging methods reach at most 2.00% Tool SR at either stage. These results show that BACAM acquires the incoming capabilities while preserving the initial WebShop capability through the first three experts.

4.3 Continual Merging Analysis

We evaluate BACAM under four expert orders: WTSA, ASTW, TWAS, and SAWT, and track SR after each integration (Figure 3). Appendix Table 8 gives the full scores.

Acquisition and retention.

In WTSA, adding Tool raises its SR from the initial WebShop expert’s 4.00% to 32.00%, while WebShop SR changes from 78.00% to 78.60%. Subsequent integrations bring Tool SR to 38.00%, while final WebShop SR is 77.20%, only 0.80 points below its initial value. Search changes from 24.10% at integration to 23.75% after ALFWorld is added. ALFWorld enters last and reaches 88.57/86.57% IID/OOD SR. BACAM does not fully acquire the ALFWorld expert’s capability at this integration stage.

Effect of merging order.

Merging order has a substantial but task-dependent effect. Final Avg SR ranges from 56.02% in SAWT to 62.82% in WTSA, a difference of 6.80 points. Across the four orders, WebShop varies by 20.40 points, whereas Search varies by only 1.68 points. The initial expert’s own-task capability is largely preserved: WebShop in WTSA ends 0.80 points below its expert, and ALFWorld in ASTW ends 2.14/0.00 points below its IID/OOD expert scores. By contrast, adding WebShop later leaves a 10.20–15.00-point gap at integration, and adding ALFWorld later leaves an 8.57–10.00-point IID gap; Tool and Search reach or approach their expert scores. Thus, order mainly affects the acquisition and subsequent retention of certain incoming capabilities rather than uniformly degrading all tasks.

Parameter adaptation.

Under TWAS, gate movement decreases across successive integrations (0.035, 0.025, and 0.013), indicating increasingly conservative updates along this sequence. MLP tensors account for 72–77% of total movement, while value projections have the largest average gate changes within attention. LayerNorm receives the tightest plasticity budgets. During ALFWorld integration, BACAM further protects WebShop more strongly than Tool in middle-layer value projections (Appendix Figure 5). These patterns show that adaptation depends on both stage and tensor type; further diagnostics appear in Appendix D.1.

4.4 Ablation on Each Component

We assess BACAM’s two levels of control after the full WebShop–Tool–Search–ALFWorld sequence (Table 2). The variants retain behavioral supervision while changing the KL directions, token weighting, or tensor-level budgets throughout merging.

(1) Task-level behavioral constraints. Using forward KL for all tasks slightly improves ALFWorld IID SR from 88.57% to 89.29%, but lowers its OOD SR from 86.57% to 85.07% and reduces Tool SR from 38.00% to 30.00%. Reverse KL for all tasks slightly improves Search SR but lowers SR on the other tasks. Neither uniform KL direction matches BACAM’s overall performance: BACAM achieves 62.82% Avg SR, compared with 60.89% for forward KL and 62.14% for reverse KL. Replacing token-group weighting with uniform token weighting reduces Avg SR to 61.40%, with the largest decreases on Tool and ALFWorld OOD. These comparisons support using different KL directions for acquisition and preservation, together with explicit weighting of behavior-critical tokens.

(2) Tensor-level plasticity budgets. Removing the conflict budget while retaining task-level constraints reduces Avg SR from 62.82% to 61.58%. The largest decrease is on Tool, from 38.00% to 34.00%; Search and ALFWorld SR also decline, while WebShop SR rises slightly from 77.20% to 77.40%. The overall improvement with the budget suggests that tensor-level conflict control complements the task-level objective, although its benefit is not uniform across tasks.

5 Conclusion

We studied continual agent merging in multi-turn interactive environments. Our method, BACAM, learns parameter-wise merging gates through task-level behavioral constraints and tensor-level conflict-aware plasticity budgets. Supervision on candidate-generated trajectories guides capability acquisition and preservation, while the budgets restrict updates in conflicting tensors. Experiments across four interactive tasks show that BACAM outperforms the evaluated merging baselines across different expert counts. In the default four-expert order, BACAM achieves 62.82% average success rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 21.69 percentage points. These findings support the promise of behavior-guided merging for interactive agents, while identifying robustness to expert merging order as a key direction for future work.

Appendix A Formal Setup and Optimization Details

A.1 Continual Merging Setup

We consider TT ordered tasks whose experts share the same architecture and tokenizer. We initialize M1=E1M_{1}=E_{1} and perform merging stages t=2,…,Tt=2,\ldots,T. At stage tt, task indices τ<t\tau<t denote previously integrated tasks and τ=t\tau=t denotes the incoming task. Each 𝒟τ\mathcal{D}_{\tau} contains unlabeled instances for task τ\tau. BACAM has access to these data and their interaction environments, the current merged model Mt−1M_{t-1}, and the incoming expert EtE_{t}. The goal is to construct a unified model MtM_{t} that acquires the capability of EtE_{t} while retaining the capabilities of Mt−1M_{t-1}:

Mt=Merge⁡(Mt−1,Et).M_{t}=\operatorname{Merge}(M_{t-1},E_{t}). (13)

This objective involves two competing requirements. Plasticity requires the merged model to acquire the incoming expert’s interactive capability, whereas stability requires it to preserve the current merged model’s behavior on earlier tasks. The stability reference is Mt−1M_{t-1}, not the discarded historical experts. Because MtM_{t} becomes the reference at the next stage, degradation can accumulate along the merging sequence.

For interactive agents, neither parameter distance nor output discrepancies on isolated histories adequately characterize this objective. An action taken early in an interaction changes the subsequent environment feedback and, consequently, the histories visited later. BACAM therefore uses candidate-generated trajectories to guide parameter merging, connecting parameter-space optimization to task-level capabilities.

A.2 Policy-Induced Interaction Trajectories

Following the ReAct paradigm (Yao et al., 2022b), we represent each interaction step as an observation–reasoning–action triplet, as illustrated in Figure 2. At step ii, the agent receives an observation oio_{i}, produces a reasoning trace rir_{i}, and executes an action aia_{i}. The environment then returns the next observation:

ri∼πθ(⋅∣hi),ai∼πθ(⋅∣hi,ri),oi+1∼ℰτ(⋅∣hi,ai),r_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{i}),\qquad a_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{i},r_{i}),\qquad o_{i+1}\sim\mathcal{E}^{\tau}(\cdot\mid h_{i},a_{i}), (14)

where hi=(o0,r0,a0,…,oi)h_{i}=(o_{0},r_{0},a_{0},\ldots,o_{i}) is the interaction history and ℰτ\mathcal{E}^{\tau} denotes the dynamics of task environment τ\tau. A complete trajectory is therefore

ξ=(o0,r0,a0,…,oL−1,rL−1,aL−1,oL).\xi=(o_{0},r_{0},a_{0},\ldots,o_{L-1},r_{L-1},a_{L-1},o_{L}). (15)

The policy and environment jointly induce the trajectory distribution

ℙπθτ​(ξ)=ρ0τ​(o0)​∏i=0L−1πθ​(ri∣hi)​πθ​(ai∣hi,ri)​ℰτ​(oi+1∣hi,ai),\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\theta}}^{\tau}(\xi)=\rho_{0}^{\tau}(o_{0})\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}\pi_{\theta}(r_{i}\mid h_{i})\pi_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid h_{i},r_{i})\mathcal{E}^{\tau}(o_{i+1}\mid h_{i},a_{i}), (16)

where ρ0τ\rho_{0}^{\tau} is the initial-observation distribution. For an autoregressive language model, the reasoning and action at step ii form a token sequence zi=(ri,ai)=(yi,1,…,yi,Li)z_{i}=(r_{i},a_{i})=(y_{i,1},\ldots,y_{i,L_{i}}), whose probability factorizes as

πθ​(ri,ai∣hi)=∏ℓ=1Liπθ​(yi,ℓ∣hi,yi,<ℓ).\pi_{\theta}(r_{i},a_{i}\mid h_{i})=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L_{i}}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,\ell}\mid h_{i},y_{i,<\ell}). (17)

The histories hih_{i} and responses ziz_{i} correspond to xix_{i} and yiy_{i} in Section 3.3. There, |ξ||\xi| counts decision points, corresponding to LL here, rather than individual observations or tokens. Agent behavior is characterized by the distribution over these interaction trajectories; an incorrect action can change the next observation and redirect subsequent decisions.

A.3 Gate and Dual Updates

At the beginning of each refresh round, the current candidate generates trajectories for the new and previously integrated tasks. These trajectories and their teacher distributions remain fixed during the gate updates in that round. Gradients are propagated through the candidate parameters but not through trajectory collection. The local conflict probe estimates the tensor budgets without updating the optimizer or dual variables, and the gate is restored before the actual updates.

For completeness, the projected dual update used for each old-task constraint is

λτ←clip⁡(λτ+ηλ​[Sτ​(g)−ϵ],0,λmax).\lambda_{\tau}\leftarrow\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\lambda_{\tau}+\eta_{\lambda}[S_{\tau}(g)-\epsilon],0,\lambda_{\max}\right). (18)

The parameterization in Equation 1 gives the gate gradient by the chain rule:

∇gℒ=Δ​θt⊙∇θtmerged​(g)ℒ.\nabla_{g}\mathcal{L}=\Delta\theta_{t}\odot\nabla_{\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g)}\mathcal{L}. (19)

The normalized descent step before applying tensor budgets is

Δ​g=−ηg​∇gℒ​(g,λ)‖∇gℒ​(g,λ)‖2.\Delta g=-\eta_{g}\frac{\nabla_{g}\mathcal{L}(g,\lambda)}{\left\|\nabla_{g}\mathcal{L}(g,\lambda)\right\|_{2}}. (20)

A.4 Derivation of the Behavioral Objectives

The two KL directions provide different signals for capability acquisition and preservation. We first derive their gradients for full-vocabulary distributions, then describe the compressed representation used in our implementation. Each derivation conditions on a fixed candidate-generated history; it does not differentiate through the environment or history sampling.

Forward KL and incoming-expert supervision.

At a fixed decision point ii and response position kk, write p=pg,i,kp=p_{g,i,k} and q=qt,i,kq=q_{t,i,k}. Let ζu\zeta_{u} be the candidate logit for vocabulary token uu, so that pu=exp⁡(ζu)/∑vexp⁡(ζv)p_{u}=\exp(\zeta_{u})/\sum_{v}\exp(\zeta_{v}). The incoming expert remains frozen. Expanding the plasticity divergence gives

DKL(q∥p)=∑uqulogqu−∑uqulogpu.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)=\sum_{u}q_{u}\log q_{u}-\sum_{u}q_{u}\log p_{u}. (21)

The first term is constant with respect to the candidate. Minimizing this divergence is therefore equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy with the expert’s soft token targets. Using ∂logpu/∂ζv=𝟏[u=v]−pv\partial\log p_{u}/\partial\zeta_{v}=\mathbf{1}[u=v]-p_{v}, we obtain

∂DKL(q∥p)∂ζv=pv−qv.\frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)}{\partial\zeta_{v}}=p_{v}-q_{v}. (22)

At the logit level, descent increases a token’s logit when pv<qvp_{v}<q_{v}. This is a distributional target, not a label for the sampled token. The expert evaluates the candidate’s history without replacing its preceding actions; the resulting signal reaches the gates through the candidate parameterization.

Reverse KL and current-model supervision.

For an old task, write q=qτ,i,kq=q_{\tau,i,k}, supplied by the frozen current merged model. The stability divergence is

DKL(p∥q)=∑upulogpuqu.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{u}p_{u}\log\frac{p_{u}}{q_{u}}. (23)

Unlike forward KL, the candidate probabilities also weight the discrepancy. Applying the softmax derivative ∂pu/∂ζv=pu(𝟏[u=v]−pv)\partial p_{u}/\partial\zeta_{v}=p_{u}(\mathbf{1}[u=v]-p_{v}) gives

∂DKL(p∥q)∂ζv=pv(logpvqv−DKL(p∥q)).\frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)}{\partial\zeta_{v}}=p_{v}\left(\log\frac{p_{v}}{q_{v}}-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\right). (24)

The logit gradient is positive when a token’s log probability ratio exceeds the candidate-weighted average ratio, so descent lowers that logit. Stability control thus discourages departures from the current model on old-task histories. Both KL directions vanish when the distributions agree, but weight disagreement differently.

Compressed distributions used in training.

For each teacher distribution qq, let KK contain its top 32 vocabulary tokens. The candidate uses the same token set. Define prest=1−∑u∈Kpup_{\mathrm{rest}}=1-\sum_{u\in K}p_{u} and qrest=1−∑u∈Kquq_{\mathrm{rest}}=1-\sum_{u\in K}q_{u}. The implemented forward divergence is

DKL(q~∥p~)=∑u∈Kqulogqupu+qrestlogqrestprest,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widetilde{q}\|\widetilde{p})=\sum_{u\in K}q_{u}\log\frac{q_{u}}{p_{u}}+q_{\mathrm{rest}}\log\frac{q_{\mathrm{rest}}}{p_{\mathrm{rest}}}, (25)

where p~\widetilde{p} and q~\widetilde{q} have 33 entries: 32 token probabilities and one remaining-vocabulary probability. The reverse divergence swaps their roles. These losses preserve the KL direction but do not distinguish tokens within the remaining vocabulary; they approximate, rather than exactly reproduce, the full-vocabulary losses derived above.

Loss aggregation across tokens and trajectories.

The aggregation in Equations 3 and 4 is a weighted sum of these token-level terms. For a token kk belonging to group BB at decision point ii in trajectory ξ\xi, its empirical weight is

wξ,i,k=1|ℛτ|​|ξ​‖ℬi‖​B|.w_{\xi,i,k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{\tau}|\,|\xi|\,|\mathcal{B}_{i}|\,|B|}. (26)

These weights sum to one over the collected task trajectories. If both token groups are present, each group receives half of a decision point’s weight, regardless of its length. Each trajectory also receives the same total weight, regardless of its number of decisions. This separates the contribution of an action span from the amount of surrounding text. It does not label actions as correct or incorrect: the supervision still comes from the appropriate teacher distribution.

A.5 Parameter Injection and Local Conflict Control

Gate gradients in parameter space.

Equation 19 follows directly from the diagonal Jacobian of the candidate parameterization:

∂θtmerged​(g)∂g=diag⁡(Δ​θt),∂ℒ∂gj=Δ​θt,j​∂ℒ∂θt,jmerged.\frac{\partial\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g)}{\partial g}=\operatorname{diag}(\Delta\theta_{t}),\qquad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial g_{j}}=\Delta\theta_{t,j}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta_{t,j}^{\mathrm{merged}}}. (27)

The gate therefore learns how much of each expert difference to inject, not an unrestricted parameter update. If the two models agree at coordinate jj, then Δ​θt,j=0\Delta\theta_{t,j}=0: changing that gate cannot change the candidate at this coordinate. More generally, equal gate changes need not imply equal parameter changes, because the expert differences can have different magnitudes.

For a gate change dhd_{h} in tensor hh, the corresponding parameter change is exactly

θt,hmerged​(gh+dh)−θt,hmerged​(gh)=dh⊙Δ​θt,h.\theta_{t,h}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g_{h}+d_{h})-\theta_{t,h}^{\mathrm{merged}}(g_{h})=d_{h}\odot\Delta\theta_{t,h}. (28)

For example, its norm is bounded by

‖dh⊙Δ​θt,h‖2≤‖Δ​θt,h‖∞​‖dh‖2.\|d_{h}\odot\Delta\theta_{t,h}\|_{2}\leq\|\Delta\theta_{t,h}\|_{\infty}\|d_{h}\|_{2}. (29)

This relation also explains why the gate diagnostics should be read alongside tensor identity and expert differences. A large gate movement identifies substantial movement along the available merging direction; it is not by itself a measure of absolute parameter displacement or task importance.

Why probe away from the current gate?

At initialization, g=𝟎g=\mathbf{0} recovers the current merged model exactly. On an old-task history, the candidate and its stability teacher then agree, yielding

Sτ​(𝟎)=0,∇gSτ​(𝟎)=𝟎.S_{\tau}(\mathbf{0})=0,\qquad\nabla_{g}S_{\tau}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}. (30)

Thus, the stability gradient at this endpoint cannot identify which acquisition directions will become harmful after leaving it. The temporary probe evaluates stability after a small step toward the incoming task. At later rounds, it similarly tests the neighborhood of the current gate rather than treating its current stability loss as a complete description of future drift.

For a small gate displacement dd supported only on tensor hh, with tensor block dhd_{h}, a first-order expansion gives

Sτ​(gprobe+d)−Sτ​(gprobe)=⟨sτ,h,dh⟩+o⁡(‖dh‖2).S_{\tau}(g_{\mathrm{probe}}+d)-S_{\tau}(g_{\mathrm{probe}})=\langle s_{\tau,h},d_{h}\rangle+o(\|d_{h}\|_{2}). (31)

Substituting dh=−α​vhd_{h}=-\alpha v_{h} with α>0\alpha>0 yields the first-order change −α⁡⟨sτ,h,vh⟩-\alpha\langle s_{\tau,h},v_{h}\rangle. A negative gradient inner product therefore indicates increased old-task drift along that acquisition direction. Equation 10 measures this opposition on fixed collected histories.

Budget range and directional restriction.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, 0≤cτ,h≤10\leq c_{\tau,h}\leq 1. Since Vh,Uτ,h≥0V_{h},U_{\tau,h}\geq 0 and δ>0\delta>0, the sensitivity factor obeys

0≤Uτ,hVh+Uτ,h+δ≤1,0≤bτ,h≤1.0\leq\frac{U_{\tau,h}}{V_{h}+U_{\tau,h}+\delta}\leq 1,\qquad 0\leq b_{\tau,h}\leq 1. (32)

Taking the minimum across old tasks preserves this range and does not average away a restrictive old-task signal. When no opposing direction is detected, cτ,h=0c_{\tau,h}=0 and the budget is one. For a fixed conflict score, stronger old-task sensitivity relative to the acquisition gradient reduces the budget.

The positive and negative parts of a gate update have disjoint support. Consequently, before the final gate clipping, Equation 12 satisfies

‖Δ​gsafe,h‖22=bh2​‖[Δ​gh]+‖22+‖[Δ​gh]−‖22≤‖Δ​gh‖22.\|\Delta g_{\mathrm{safe},h}\|_{2}^{2}=b_{h}^{2}\|[\Delta g_{h}]_{+}\|_{2}^{2}+\|[\Delta g_{h}]_{-}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\Delta g_{h}\|_{2}^{2}. (33)

The budget reduces only the component that increases the incoming expert’s contribution. A negative gate update reduces that contribution and remains available for stability recovery. This directional rule is distinct from scaling the entire tensor gradient, which would also suppress movement back toward the current merged model. Clipping then keeps every parameter within the coordinate-wise interval between the two frozen models. The resulting restriction bounds parameter injection; it does not establish monotonic improvement in task success.

Appendix B Experimental Protocol and Merging Configurations

B.1 Evaluation Protocol

All models are evaluated on the same fixed sets. For WebShop, we evaluate agents on 500 synthetic shopping goals using a set of 1,000 products; an episode succeeds when its task score reaches 1.0. BFCL v3 uses 100 held-out multi_turn_base tasks and the official checker: every turn must pass its state and response checks. MuSiQue uses 2,017 held-out questions; Search success requires normalized substring matching of the final answer (Sub-EM). ALFWorld uses all 140 valid_seen games for IID and 134 valid_unseen games for OOD evaluation. Round is the mean number of interaction steps across all WebShop or ALFWorld episodes, including failures. Table 3 gives the generation settings for each benchmark.

Metric calculation and interpretation.

Let nn be the number of evaluation instances and sj∈{0,1}s_{j}\in\{0,1\} the success indicator for instance jj, determined by the corresponding evaluator. The reported success rate is

SR=100n​∑j=1nsj.\mathrm{SR}=\frac{100}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}s_{j}. (34)

For WebShop, let rj∈[0,1]r_{j}\in[0,1] be the terminal task score. Then sj=𝟏[rj=1]s_{j}=\mathbf{1}[r_{j}=1], whereas the continuous score is

TS=100n​∑j=1nrj.\mathrm{TS}=\frac{100}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}r_{j}. (35)

TS gives credit for partial satisfaction of shopping constraints, while SR requires full completion. A high TS with a lower SR can therefore indicate that an agent identifies an appropriate product but fails to satisfy a remaining constraint. These metrics are complementary, not interchangeable.

For BFCL, sjs_{j} represents success on the complete multi-turn instance, rather than the fraction of individual calls that pass a check. For Search, it represents a matched final answer; it does not separately grade each retrieval. ALFWorld success is determined by completing the environment goal. We use the common SR label while preserving these benchmark-specific success criteria.

For WebShop and ALFWorld, if ljl_{j} is the number of interaction steps taken before success or termination, then

Round=1n​∑j=1nlj.\mathrm{Round}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}l_{j}. (36)

Failures remain in this average. A shorter interaction can reflect efficient completion, but it can also reflect early termination without success. Conversely, a larger Round can result from repeated unsuccessful actions. We therefore interpret interaction length together with SR and, for WebShop, TS, rather than treating a reduction in Round alone as a performance gain.

The main four-expert average assigns equal weight to the five reported SR columns, including ALFWorld IID and OOD separately. It summarizes performance across these evaluation conditions; it is not the success rate obtained by pooling their instances. The latter would weight Search much more heavily because its evaluation set is larger. Two- and three-expert averages use only the task columns included in their respective blocks.

B.2 Merging Configurations

BACAM optimization.

Table 4 reports the settings shared by the four measured orders. These runs differ in expert arrival order. A training state is one decision point (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) extracted from a candidate-generated trajectory, not a complete episode. Training inputs are unlabeled; teachers provide the token-distribution targets. We use the Top-32 representation in Equation 25 with distillation temperature 1.0.

Baseline configurations.

Table 5 distinguishes task-instance access from the optimization signal in our implementations. RAM and RAM++ use only task-vector statistics, whereas WUDI-Merging and NUFILT optimize objectives derived from model parameters without task instances. AdaMerging and AdaMerging++ use first-turn prompts without multi-turn environment rollouts. Expert Merging and BACAM both use teacher outputs, but on expert-generated and candidate-generated trajectories, respectively. No ground-truth response labels are used for merging, and all calibration instances are separate from the held-out evaluation set. Data-collection and update schedules are method-specific, not budget-matched.

Appendix D Gate and Conflict Diagnostics

D.1 TWAS Order

Under TWAS, gate movement declines across integrations. MLP tensors account for most movement, while attention gains share as the sequence progresses. Budgets vary across capabilities and stages: they restrict updates toward the incoming expert, not movement back toward the current model. Gate movement and budgets describe optimization behavior, rather than directly measuring a tensor’s importance for task success.

Appendix E Qualitative Examples

The examples compare BACAM with WUDI-Merging on matched evaluation instances. Each example summarizes the decisive observation–reasoning–action step; reasoning is paraphrased from the recorded trajectory rather than quoted verbatim.

Across these matched examples, BACAM follows the remaining task constraints and environment feedback at the decisive step, whereas WUDI-Merging diverges before completion.
